entries.title: About Us & Institutional Governance — Crypto Service Suite
entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Governance & Engineering Philosophy About Us & Institutional Governance — Crypto Service Suite Crypto Service Suite is an open-source TypeScript monorepo with enforced test coverage gates, a small set of well-known runtime dependencies, and self-hostable deployment. The Sovereign Infrastructure Mandate Modern enterprise architectures cannot outsource their foundational cryptographic trust to third-party hosted black-boxes or custodial intermediaries. Custodial dependency introduces counterparty solvency risk, regulatory exposure, and single points of operational failure. Crypto Service Suite is open-source software you can run on your own infrastructure, on-premises or in a private cloud. It does not integrate with hardware security modules (HSMs): the crypto-kms PKCS#11 provider is an in-memory software simulation for tests. The Four-Layer Monorepo Architecture The suite is divided into 18 specialized, decoupled packages maintained in a strict monorepo moving in lockstep semantic versioning: LAYER 1 // FOUNDATION Core Primitives @sebastienrousseau/crypto-lib implements FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms (via @noble/post-quantum; not a validated cryptographic module) and classical ciphers built on the @noble/* libraries and OpenPGP.js. @sebastienrousseau/crypto-wasm is a placeholder and contains no WebAssembly code yet. LAYER 2 // INFRASTRUCTURE & ORM KMS, Edge & Database Field Encryption @sebastienrousseau/crypto-kms, crypto-edge, crypto-prisma, and crypto-typeorm provide a unified KMS interface (AWS and local providers implemented; GCP, Azure and Vault are stubs), edge runtime support (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Deno, Bun, browsers), and transparent database column encryption. LAYER 3 // PROTOCOLS & CLIENTS Servers, APIs, SDK & UI Integrations @sebastienrousseau/crypto-server, crypto-api, crypto-cli, crypto-sdk, crypto-react, and crypto-vue expose a Fastify REST service, a zero-dependency fetch-based SDK client, an interactive CLI, and reactive frontend hooks. LAYER 4 // ASSURANCE & AI Regulatory Auditing, IDE Static Analysis & AI Tooling @sebastienrousseau/crypto-cbom, crypto-lsp, crypto-mcp, crypto-benchmarks, and crypto-testing deliver CycloneDX 1.6 and SPDX 3.0 cryptographic bills of materials, Language Server Protocol linting, Model Context Protocol server tools, benchmarking harnesses, and test fixtures. Engineering Discipline & Verification Gates Quality Gates and Known Limits Coverage gates: CI enforces 100% line and function coverage in every package (mocha and c8), and 100% branch coverage in every package except crypto-lib (99.5%). Memory zeroization is limited: crypto-lib exports wipeMemory() and SecureBuffer, but its own APIs do not call them, and keys passed as hex strings cannot be wiped. No constant-time guarantee: The implementations have not been formally verified against timing side channels. @noble/post-quantum does not guarantee constant-time execution. Licensing and supply chain: Dual-licensed under Apache 2.0 and MIT. CI generates a software bill of materials (SBOM) and runs pnpm audit and CodeQL. Regulation: The suite provides building blocks, such as a CycloneDX CBOM generator, that can support DORA (EU 2022/2554) work. Using it does not make a system DORA compliant. Engage with the Maintainers Learn how fintechs, banks, and enterprise engineering teams leverage Crypto Service Suite for sovereign cryptographic operations. How do Crypto Service and Hedera Hashgraph complement each other in enterprise stacks? Enterprises frequently confuse public distributed ledgers like Hedera with foundational cryptographic libraries. While Hedera provides decentralized ordering and timestamping, Crypto Service Suite provides the quantum-safe cryptographic operating system securing enterprise applications across any layer (L0, L1, L2, or traditional private banking clouds). Multi-Backend Interoperability: Write cryptographic payloads once and target Hedera, EVM chains, or relational databases seamlessly. entries.title: 2027 Post-Quantum Strategic Horizon & Cryptographic Audit
entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ White Paper // Academic & Strategic Research 2027 Post-Quantum Strategic Horizon & Cryptographic Audit An exhaustive technical white paper analyzing quantum cryptanalysis timelines, lattice-based algorithms, DORA ICT risk requirements, and sovereign cryptographic resilience. Table of Contents 1. Executive Synthesis & The 2027 Threat Landscape 2. Threat Modeling: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) 3. Mathematical Foundations of Lattice Cryptography 4. Empirical Micro-Benchmarks & Throughput Analysis 5. Side-Channel & Fault-Injection Countermeasures 6. Strategic 2025–2027 Institutional Transition Roadmap 7. Post-Quantum Migration Architecture & Interbank Rails 1. Executive Synthesis & The 2027 Threat Landscape The global technological architecture is undergoing its most profound cryptographic restructuring in half a century. The mathematical assumptions underpinning modern security—namely, the intractability of integer factorization (RSA) and discrete logarithms over elliptic curves (ECDSA, Ed25519)—will be decisively compromised by Cryptanalytically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) running Shor's algorithm. While fault-tolerant quantum computers capable of breaking RSA-2048 in polynomial time remain a multi-year engineering challenge, the security threshold for long-lived sensitive communications has already expired. Financial contracts, corporate IP, sensitive customer records, and regulatory archives carry legal lifespans ranging from 10 to 30 years. Any encrypted message transmitted over public networks today is subject to exfiltration and archival. 2. Threat Modeling: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) Under the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) attack paradigm, adversary intelligence agencies and sophisticated cyber syndicates intercept encrypted high-value enterprise traffic today, storing the raw ciphertext in petabyte-scale data repositories. Once a CRQC becomes operational, all historic key exchanges (such as Diffie-Hellman and ECDH) are trivially broken, exposing: Encrypted database backups, customer records, and long-term transaction ledgers. Sovereign credentials, API secrets, and cloud infrastructure keys. Institutional master key derivation material and long-term root secrets. Customer personally identifiable information (PII) subject to GDPR, HIPAA, and financial secrecy mandates. Consequently, US National Security Memorandum 10 (NSM-10) directs federal agencies to inventory and migrate quantum-vulnerable cryptography, and the ICT risk management requirements of the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) lead many financial institutions to plan a transition to hybrid or post-quantum algorithms for long-lived data. 3. Mathematical Foundations of Lattice Cryptography NIST's standardized post-quantum algorithms (FIPS 203, FIPS 204, and FIPS 205) are founded on the geometric hardness of high-dimensional lattices. Unlike RSA and ECC, lattice problems have no known sub-exponential quantum algorithms. Module Learning With Errors (M-LWE) The core mathematical engine of ML-KEM (FIPS 203). Operates over polynomial rings $R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^n + 1)$, where $n = 256$ and $q = 3329$. Provides worst-case to average-case hardness reductions to standard lattice problems such as SIVP (Shortest Independent Vectors Problem). Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) Polynomial multiplications in $R_q$ are computed in $O(n \log n)$ time using negative wrapped convolution via NTT. Crypto Service does not implement this arithmetic itself: crypto-lib calls @noble/post-quantum, which is not independently audited and does not guarantee constant-time execution. Module Short Integer Solution (M-SIS) The security foundation of ML-DSA (FIPS 204). Guarantees unforgeability against chosen-message attacks under the hardness of finding short vectors in a random module lattice, with rejection sampling ensuring signatures leak no secret state. Stateless Hash-Based Signatures (SLH-DSA) Standardized in FIPS 205. Rely exclusively on the collision-resistance of cryptographic hash functions (SHAKE-256 and SHA-2). Acts as a conservative fallback if unexpected structural breakthroughs occur in lattice theory. 4. Sizes and Benchmarks The main cost of moving to lattice-based algorithms is size: ML-KEM ciphertexts and ML-DSA signatures are much larger than their elliptic-curve counterparts. The sizes below are fixed by the standards. Timing figures previously shown here did not come from committed benchmark code and have been withdrawn; run node benchmarks/crypto-bench.ts from the repository to measure on your own hardware. Algorithm Type NIST Level Ciphertext / Sig Size ML-KEM-768 PQ Lattice KEM Level 3 (AES-192) 1,088 bytes RSA-3072 Classical Factorization Level 3 Equivalent 384 bytes X25519 Classical Curve Level 1 Equivalent 32 bytes Hybrid KEM (X25519 + ML-KEM-768, library-specific combiner) Dual-Key Hybrid Dual Classical + PQ 1,120 bytes ML-DSA-65 PQ

AWS KMS and a local provider are implemented; GCP, Azure and Vault are stubs. 04 Database & Middleware Encryption Transparent column-level encryption for Prisma ORM, TypeORM, and Express/Fastify request middleware. 05 Edge Runtime Support Web Crypto adapter for Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Deno, Bun and browsers. 06 CBOM, LSP & AI Agent Tooling CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM generator for cryptographic inventories, Language Server Protocol, and Model Context Protocol (MCP). Developer Quick-Start Installation npm (0.0.8 or later) # 1. Install (0.0.8 or later) pnpm add @sebastienrousseau/crypto-lib // 2. ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation (FIPS 203 algorithm) import { mlKemKeygen, mlKemEncap, mlKemDecap } from "@sebastienrousseau/crypto-lib"; const kem = mlKemKeygen(768); const { ciphertext, sharedSecret } = mlKemEncap(768, kem.publicKey); const received = mlKemDecap(768, kem.secretKey, ciphertext); SOLUTION 01 // CORE CRYPTOGRAPHY 1. Post-Quantum Enclaves & Hybrid Key Encapsulation A cryptographically relevant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and elliptic-curve cryptography. You can start using NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) algorithms today; crypto-lib implements them via @noble/post-quantum, which is not a validated cryptographic module. Under the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) attack model, state actors record encrypted traffic today for future decryption. Hybrid schemes are designed so that an adversary must break both the classical and the lattice component to recover the shared secret. FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) Algorithms @sebastienrousseau/crypto-lib exposes ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 through @noble/post-quantum. ML-KEM-768 targets NIST security category 3 and has 1,088-byte ciphertexts. Composite Dual-Layer Hybrid Schemes Combines a classical curve (X25519, NIST P-256 or X448) with ML-KEM and derives the session key from both shared secrets, so an attacker must break both components to recover it. FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) Digital Signatures Lattice-based digital signatures (ML-DSA-44/65/87) via @noble/post-quantum. ML-DSA-65 targets NIST security category 3. @noble/post-quantum does not guarantee constant-time execution. Memory Hygiene & Entropy Randomness comes from the platform CSPRNG. crypto-lib exports wipeMemory() and SecureBuffer for callers, but its own APIs do not zeroize intermediate state, and keys passed as hex strings cannot be wiped. SOLUTION 02 // MICROSERVICE ARCHITECTURE 2. Sovereign Crypto-as-a-Service Daemon & Client SDK Third-party hosted platforms introduce counterparty risk and vendor lock-in. Crypto Service Suite lets you run a self-hosted CaaS tier in your private cloud or on-premises data centre. Your applications call the service over a REST API. Keys you manage with it stay on infrastructure you control. Fastify REST Microservice @sebastienrousseau/crypto-server exposes crypto-lib operations behind documented REST endpoints, with rate limiting and OpenTelemetry instrumentation. No throughput figures are published yet. Type-Safe Zero-Dependency SDK @sebastienrousseau/crypto-sdk is a zero-dependency, fetch-based TypeScript client with typed request and response bindings. Interactive CLI The @sebastienrousseau/crypto-cli package offers key pair generation, encryption, signing, hashing and CBOM generation from an interactive terminal menu. It has no non-interactive flags, so it is not suited to scripts or CI pipelines. Self-Hosted Deployment Run the service inside your private VPC or on-premises infrastructure. OpenTelemetry export is off unless you set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT. SOLUTION 03 // KEY MANAGEMENT 3. KMS Interface @sebastienrousseau/crypto-kms defines one TypeScript interface for key management backends. Today the AWS KMS and local in-memory providers are implemented. The Google Cloud, Azure and HashiCorp Vault providers are stubs that reject every call with Not implemented. generateDataKey() supports envelope encryption: data encryption keys (DEKs) are wrapped by a key encryption key (KEK) held by the provider. AWS KMS (implemented) AwsKmsProvider calls AWS Key Management Service through @aws-sdk/client-kms. There is no direct CloudHSM integration. Google Cloud KMS (stub) GcpKmsProvider exists as an interface

entries.title: Transparent Column-Level Database Encryption with Prisma & TypeORM
entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Database Security White Paper · ORM Field Encryption Transparent Column-Level Database Encryption with Prisma & TypeORM An architectural guide to authenticated field-level encryption in application code with the Prisma and TypeORM adapters, including their current limits. Sebastien Rousseau · Architecture Practice Document ID: CSS-DATA-2026-007 Classification: Technical Engineering White Paper Supported ORMs: Prisma Client (extensions and middleware) · TypeORM Executive Abstract Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) at the storage layer protects against theft of disks and snapshots, but anyone who can query the database still reads plaintext. Application-level field encryption closes that gap by encrypting sensitive values before they leave application memory. @sebastienrousseau/crypto-prisma and @sebastienrousseau/crypto-typeorm provide this for Prisma and TypeORM. Both encrypt configured fields with XChaCha20-Poly1305 (crypto-lib's secretbox) under a single 256-bit key supplied by the application. An earlier version of this paper described AES-256-GCM envelope encryption with ML-KEM-768 key wrapping, KMS-backed key rotation, a crypto-cli db rekey command, Drizzle support and measured query overheads; none of that exists in the code, and those claims have been withdrawn. Table of Contents 1. Limits of Disk-Level TDE 2. How the Adapters Encrypt Fields 3. Prisma Client Extension 4. TypeORM Column Decorator 5. Key Management and Rotation 6. Performance 7. Migrating Existing Data 1. Limits of Disk-Level TDE Storage-volume encryption and database TDE protect data on disk. They do not protect against: Over-privileged access: any account with SELECT permission reads sensitive columns in plaintext. SQL injection: the engine decrypts blocks for every query, so an injection returns plaintext rows. Replicas, logs and dumps: replication streams, query logs and exports may contain plaintext values. Encrypting sensitive fields in the application means the database only stores ciphertext for those fields. 2. How the Adapters Encrypt Fields Key: the application supplies one 256-bit key as a 64-character hex string. The adapters do not fetch or wrap keys through a KMS. Encryption: each configured value is serialised to UTF-8 and sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305 using a random 24-byte nonce. Encoding: the stored value is base64 of nonce || ciphertext || tag, so the column must be a text type large enough to hold it. Searchable fields (Prisma only): fields listed as deterministic are stored as an HMAC-SHA256 of the value instead. They support equality lookups but cannot be decrypted. 3. Prisma Client Extension createFieldEncryptionExtension() returns a Prisma Client extension ($extends); createEncryptionMiddleware() offers the older $use style. import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client"; import { createFieldEncryptionExtension } from "@sebastienrousseau/crypto-prisma"; export const prisma = new PrismaClient().$extends( createFieldEncryptionExtension({ key: process.env.FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY!, // 64 hex characters encryptedFields: [ { model: "AccountHolder", fields: ["nationalId", "bankAccountNumber"] }, ], deterministicFields: ["nationalId"], // HMAC, searchable, not decryptable }), ); The algorithm option is accepted but ignored: values are always sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305. 4. TypeORM Column Decorator @sebastienrousseau/crypto-typeorm provides an @EncryptedColumn() decorator backed by a column transformer, and an EncryptionSubscriber: import { Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn, Column } from "typeorm"; import { EncryptedColumn } from "@sebastienrousseau/crypto-typeorm"; @Entity() export class CorporateTreasuryAccount { @PrimaryGeneratedColumn("uuid") id: string; @Column() legalEntityName: string; // Key from options.encrypt.key or the TYPEORM_ENCRYPTION_KEY env var @EncryptedColumn({ encrypt: { key: process.env.COLUMN_ENCRYPTION_KEY! } }) beneficiaryRoutingNumber: string; } 5. Key Management and Rotation The adapters take a raw key from the application. They have no KMS integration, no key versioning in the stored value, and no rotation tooling. To rotate a key today, read each row with the old key and write it back with the new one in an application-level migration. If you need envelope encryption, generate and unwrap data keys with @sebastienrousseau/crypto-kms (AWS KMS is implemented) and pass the unwrapped key to the adapter. 6. Performance No query-overhead measurements are published. The table in earlier versions of this paper did not come from committed benchmark code and has been withdrawn. Measure the overhead in your own environment before adopting the adapters on hot paths. 7. Migrating Existing Data When the Prisma adapter cannot decrypt a stored value (for example, a legacy plaintext row), it returns the stored value unchanged. That behaviour allows a gradual migration: Change the target column to a text type large enough for the base64

entries.title: CBOM Manual: Cryptographic Inventories for DORA Work
entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Implementation Guide · DORA & CBOM CBOM Manual: Cryptographic Inventories for DORA Work How to generate CycloneDX 1.6 Cryptographic Bills of Materials with crypto-cbom and use them as inventory input for Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) work. A CBOM does not by itself establish compliance. Sebastien Rousseau · Governance, Risk & Compliance Document ID: CSS-COMP-2026-005 Classification: Implementation Guide Context: EU DORA (Regulation 2022/2554) ICT risk management Standard: CycloneDX v1.6 CBOM · SPDX 3.0 Executive Abstract The EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) requires financial entities to maintain an ICT risk management framework, and its regulatory technical standards include requirements on encryption and cryptographic key management. Knowing which algorithms your systems use is a practical first step. This guide shows how to produce that inventory as a CycloneDX 1.6 Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) with @sebastienrousseau/crypto-cbom, and how to flag weak algorithms in CI. It is not legal advice. Generating a CBOM does not make a system DORA compliant, and the tool has not been assessed by any supervisor or auditor. An earlier version of this guide attributed specific obligations and penalties to DORA Articles 13 and 14 and described features (SARIF output, evidence bundles, key-rotation proofs) that do not exist; those statements have been withdrawn. Table of Contents 1. Where a Cryptographic Inventory Fits 2. What a CBOM Contains 3. Generating and Auditing a CBOM in CI 4. Algorithm Classification Used by the Audit 5. Third-Party Providers 6. What the Tool Produces 7. A Practical Starting Checklist 1. Where a Cryptographic Inventory Fits DORA's ICT risk management requirements, and the regulatory technical standards made under it, expect financial entities to manage encryption and cryptographic keys deliberately. Check the regulation and the standards themselves, or your legal and compliance teams, for the exact obligations that apply to you. Whatever the precise obligations, you cannot manage algorithms you have not inventoried. A CBOM gives a machine-readable list of the algorithms found in your code that you can review, track over time and feed into your own risk processes. 2. What a CBOM Contains A CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM lists cryptographic assets as components with crypto-properties, such as the primitive, parameter set and the functions used. crypto-cbom builds these entries from the algorithm names it finds when scanning source files. The /v2/compliance/cbom endpoint of crypto-server returns a CBOM of the algorithms that service implements. 3. Generating and Auditing a CBOM in CI Install @sebastienrousseau/crypto-cbom from npm (0.0.8 or later). Its CLI has two commands: scan writes a CycloneDX (or, with --format spdx, SPDX) CBOM, and audit validates a CBOM and prints an audit. crypto-cbom scan src/ --format cyclonedx --output cbom.cdx.json crypto-cbom audit cbom.cdx.json Because audit exits with status 1 when the inventory fails its checks, you can run it as a CI step to stop a pull request that introduces broken algorithms. It prints JSON; it does not produce SARIF or line-level annotations. 4. Algorithm Classification Used by the Audit The audit classifies each asset by name. This is a heuristic based on the algorithm name, not a regulatory classification: Algorithm names matched Audit classification Suggested replacement MD5, SHA-1, DES/3DES, RC4, ECB Broken or deprecated SHA-256/SHA-512; AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 RSA, ECC, ECDSA, Ed25519 Vulnerable to a future quantum computer Hybrid or post-quantum KEMs (ML-KEM) and signatures (ML-DSA) AES-128, CBC mode Transitional AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 Other names (for example ML-KEM, ML-DSA) Not flagged None 5. Third-Party Providers DORA also covers the management of ICT third-party risk. When you depend on external software or service providers, consider asking them for a CBOM with each major release and for their post-quantum migration plans, so their cryptography can be included in your own inventory. 6. What the Tool Produces crypto-cbom scan: a CycloneDX 1.6 or SPDX 3.0 CBOM document. crypto-cbom audit: a JSON audit result with findings per asset and a summary score. There is no evidence bundle, key-rotation proof or auditor package. Treat the output as engineering input to be reviewed by people accountable for your compliance. 7. A Practical Starting Checklist Discover: run crypto-cbom scan across your repositories and collect the CBOMs. Review: check the findings by hand; name-based scanning misses indirect uses and can flag false positives. Remediate: remove broken algorithms (DES/3DES, RC4, MD5, SHA-1) from active use. Plan: record where quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are used and plan their migration with your risk and compliance teams. Preferred Citation: Rousseau, S. (2026). entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Threat Intelligence White Paper · HNDL Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL): Defending Long-Dated Enterprise Assets An exhaustive architectural analysis detailing adversarial traffic interception, long-term cryptographic decay, and immediate hybrid post-quantum defenses. Published September 28, 2026 · Sebastien Rousseau · Threat Intelligence & Vulnerability Directorate Document ID: CSS-THREAT-2026-002 Classification: Threat Intelligence Treatise Threat Actor Tier: Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) / Sovereign Signals Intelligence Primary Countermeasure: Hybrid Key Encapsulation (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) Executive Abstract The most dangerous vector in modern cyber warfare does not involve immediate ransomware deployment, unauthorized database exfiltration, or denial-of-service disruptions. It is entirely silent. Under the Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) attack paradigm, adversary state actors and cyber syndicates are systematically intercepting and archiving petabytes of encrypted corporate traffic traversing public transit networks, cloud cross-connects, and undersea optical cables. Because financial transactions, sovereign debt portfolios, clinical healthcare data, and proprietary intellectual property possess legal and competitive lifespans exceeding 10 to 30 years, communications harvested today will remain catastrophic liabilities when early Cryptanalytically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) become operational. This technical paper models adversarial storage costs, quantum cryptanalytic timelines, and concrete mathematical engineering patterns to eliminate retroactive exposure today. Table of Contents 1. Adversary Doctrine: Petabyte-Scale Harvesting Economics 2. The Exposure Calculus of Long-Dated Enterprise Assets 3. Cryptographic Decay Curves: Classical Diffie-Hellman vs. Shor's Algorithm 4. Mathematical Architecture of Hybrid Dual-Key Encapsulation 5. Defending Data-at-Rest: Retroactive Decryption of Encrypted Database Backups 6. Implementation Patterns Using Crypto Service Suite 7. Executive Takeaways & Priority Remediation Checklist 1. Adversary Doctrine: Petabyte-Scale Harvesting Economics State intelligence agencies operate with decades-long planning horizons. The economic cost of capturing and storing encrypted enterprise traffic has plummeted over the past decade: Storage Commodity Costs: High-density tape libraries and object storage allow archiving raw ciphertext at less than $0.001 per gigabyte per month. Targeted Interception Chokepoints: Traffic traversing major Internet Exchange Points (IXPs), cloud interconnects, and inter-datacenter fiber links is passively tapped via optical splitters without disrupting line-rate latency. Automated Metadata Indexing: Intercepted packets are classified by domain, TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), certificates, and target institution, creating an indexed catalog awaiting future quantum cryptanalytic compute. Adversaries do not need to break encryption in real time; they need only wait until quantum factorization costs fall below the intelligence value of the stored data. 2. The Exposure Calculus of Long-Dated Enterprise Assets Most enterprise security architectures mistakenly treat data confidentiality as an ephemeral requirement. In reality, data value persists far longer than cryptographic algorithm longevity: Enterprise Asset Category Statutory Retention Lifespan Current Protection Mechanism Quantum Compromise Impact Interbank Settlement & SWIFT Logs 20–30 Years (Basel III / AML) RSA-2048 / ECDSA P-256 Complete retroactive ledger exposure; sovereign currency destabilization Corporate M&A & Strategic Deal Rooms 10–15 Years Classical TLS 1.3 (ECDHE) Insider trading exposure; corporate espionage Institutional Custody & Master Keys Indefinite / Permanent PKCS#11 HSM RSA-4096 Exfiltration of digital asset reserves and sovereign key material Health Records & Clinical Trials 25–50 Years (HIPAA / GDPR) AES-GCM with RSA-wrapped KEK Catastrophic breach of patient privacy and biopharmaceutical IP 3. Cryptographic Decay Curves: Classical Diffie-Hellman vs. Shor's Algorithm When an enterprise exchanges keys using classical Diffie-Hellman (DH) or Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH), the shared secret $K$ is computed as: $$K = g^{ab} \pmod p \quad \text{or} \quad K = a \cdot (b \cdot G)$$ An adversary observing public keys $A = g^a$ and $B = g^b$ records these values alongside the encrypted payload. On a classical computer, extracting $a$ or $b$ requires solving the discrete logarithm problem—computationally infeasible ($\sim 2^{128}$ operations for secp256r1). However, Shor's quantum algorithm evaluates modular exponentiation across quantum superpositions: $$\mathcal{O}((\log N)^2 \cdot \log(\log N) \cdot \log(\log(\log N)))$$ With approximately 4,000 logical qubits operating under fault-tolerant quantum error correction, an adversary will reconstruct the private exponent $a$ in mere seconds.

entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Interbank Infrastructure Brief · ISO 20022 & SWIFT Post-Quantum Migration Architecture & Interbank Settlement Rails Transitioning wholesale banking settlement engines, ISO 20022 payment payloads, and high-throughput SWIFT/Fedwire rails to quantum-resistant signatures with zero downtime. Published September 28, 2026 · Sebastien Rousseau · Wholesale Payments Practice Document ID: CSS-RAILS-2026-003 Classification: Interbank Architecture Specification Protocols: ISO 20022 (pacs.008 / pacs.009 / pain.001) · SWIFT FINplus · Fedwire · CHIPS Standards: NIST FIPS 203 / FIPS 204 · W3C XML Signature 2.0 Executive Abstract The worldwide migration of wholesale payment rails to the ISO 20022 standard represents the largest structural transformation in financial messaging history. However, the cryptographic security of ISO 20022 payment payloads (`pacs.008.001.10`, `pacs.009.001.10`) currently relies on classical digital signatures (W3C XML Signature with RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256) and classical transport layer encryption. Transitioning core settlement engines to post-quantum cryptography introduces unique engineering constraints: digital signature sizes increase by more than 50x (from 64 bytes in ECDSA to 3,309 bytes in NIST ML-DSA-65), while high-throughput clearing engines must verify tens of thousands of payment instructions per second under strict sub-second settlement Service Level Agreements (SLAs). This technical paper specifies an operational migration architecture for Tier-1 banks, payment system operators, and clearing houses. It formulates a backwards-compatible dual-signature envelope format, specifies batch verification mechanisms, and demonstrates how financial institutions can transition critical payment corridors with zero downtime. Table of Contents 1. The High-Throughput Interbank Settlement Landscape 2. The Cryptographic Anatomy of ISO 20022 Payloads 3. The Signature Size Dilemma: Managing 3.3 KB ML-DSA Signatures 4. The Backwards-Compatible Dual-Signature Envelope Format 5. High-Throughput Batch Verification & Latency SLAs 6. Rail-by-Rail Migration Strategy (SWIFT, Fedwire, RTGS) 7. Summary & Implementation Roadmap for Bank Payments Architecture Teams 1. The High-Throughput Interbank Settlement Landscape Global interbank settlement systems operate under the most stringent availability requirements in software engineering: 99.999% uptime, zero message loss, deterministic ordering, and sub-second clearing. Every payment message traversing SWIFT, the Federal Reserve's Fedwire Funds Service, the Clearing House Interbank Payments System (CHIPS), or the Eurosystem's TARGET2 requires cryptographic non-repudiation: Origin Authentication: Verifying that the sending financial institution strictly authorized the debit instruction. Payload Integrity: Ensuring that beneficiary account numbers, IBANs, amounts, and currency codes have not been altered in transit. Non-Repudiation: Guaranteeing that neither counterparty can contest the legal validity of the settlement event before central bank clearing authorities. 2. The Cryptographic Anatomy of ISO 20022 Payloads An ISO 20022 financial message comprises a Business Application Header (`head.001.001.03`) and a Document Body (such as `pacs.008.001.10` for customer credit transfers): <!-- Simplified ISO 20022 pacs.008 Payload with Cryptographic Envelope --> <BusinessMessageEnvelope xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:head.001.001.03"> <AppHdr> <Fr><FIId><FinInstnId><BICFI>HSBCGB2LXXX</BICFI></FinInstnId></FIId></Fr> <To><FIId><FinInstnId><BICFI>BARCGB22XXX</BICFI></FinInstnId></FIId></To> <BizMsgIdr>B20260928-98421092</BizMsgIdr> <MsgDefIdr>pacs.008.001.10</MsgDefIdr> <CreDt>2026-09-28T09:14:00Z</CreDt> </AppHdr> <Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pacs.008.001.10"> <FIToFICstmrCdtTrf> <GrpHdr><MsgId>HSBC-20260928-001</MsgId></GrpHdr> <CdtTrfTxInf> <IntrBkSttlmAmt Ccy="EUR">15000000.00</IntrBkSttlmAmt> </CdtTrfTxInf> </FIToFICstmrCdtTrf> </Document> <!-- Cryptographic Security Header --> <Sgntr> <!-- Classical ECDSA + Post-Quantum ML-DSA-65 Dual Signature --> </Sgntr> </BusinessMessageEnvelope> 3. The Signature Size Dilemma: Managing 3.3 KB ML-DSA Signatures In classical payment engineering, digital signatures represent a negligible fraction of the message footprint: an ECDSA P-256 signature occupies 64 bytes. In contrast, NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 signatures require 3,309 bytes. If attached directly to individual micro-messages, this creates severe network operational complications: TCP Packet Fragmentation: Standard Ethernet maximum transmission units (MTU) are 1,500 bytes. A 3.3 KB signature forces a single ISO 20022 message across three IP packets, multiplying packet loss probabilities and triggering reassembly delays on high-speed gateway interfaces. Database Bloat in Settlement Archives: Processing 50 million transactions daily increases annual storage requirements by over 60

Published September 2025 · Sebastien Rousseau · Emerging Payments Association Asia (EPAA) Quantum-Safe Working Group Document ID: EPAA-QSP-2025-01 Classification: Public Industry Treatise Target Rails: SWIFT · RTGS · ISO 20022 · Instant Payments Status: Published Executive Abstract Quantum computing threatens the foundational cryptographic algorithms securing global financial services. From wholesale interbank settlement to domestic instant payments, the infrastructure of commerce relies on asymmetric mathematical primitives—predominantly RSA and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC)—that will be rendered completely obsolete once a Cryptanalytically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) is realized. Because adversaries are actively executing Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) attacks against enterprise communication channels, the window for strategic preparation is not ten years away: it is present today. This paper outlines the systemic exposure of payment rails across the Asia-Pacific region and global clearing houses, detailing the structural requirements for post-quantum cryptographic migration aligned with NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA). It argues for immediate industry coordination focused on cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM) inventories, dual-layer hybrid protocol encapsulation, and crypto-agility across core banking settlement engines. Table of Contents 1. The Quantum Threat Horizon to Interbank Rails 2. Vulnerability Assessment Across Payment Rails (SWIFT, RTGS, ACH) 3. The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) Threat to Settlement Logs 4. NIST PQC Standards & Algorithmic Transitions (FIPS 203/204/205) 5. Operational Payload Constraints & ISO 20022 Message Engineering 6. Actionable Five-Stage Institutional Migration Blueprint 7. Policy Recommendations for Central Banks & Scheme Operators 1. The Quantum Threat Horizon to Interbank Rails The global financial system transfers over $5 trillion daily across domestic Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) schemes, interbank networks, and cross-border payment corridors. Every transaction, clearing message, and liquidity movement relies upon cryptographic integrity guarantees established in the late 20th century. The mathematical foundation of these guarantees rests upon the computational difficulty of two problems: integer factorisation (the basis of RSA) and the discrete logarithm problem over elliptic curve groups (ECDSA, Ed25519, ECDH). In 1994, Peter Shor formulated a quantum algorithm demonstrating that a quantum computer operating with sufficient coherent physical qubits can solve both problems in polynomial time ($\mathcal{O}((\log N)^3)$). Recent empirical advances in quantum error correction, neutral-atom qubit architectures, and topological qubit designs indicate that the threshold for cryptanalytically relevant quantum computation is compressing. Leading intelligence assessments (including the US NSA CNSA 2.0 timeline and the UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance) project that high-value symmetric and asymmetric infrastructure must transition to post-quantum algorithms between 2025 and 2030 to prevent systemic systemic failure. 2. Vulnerability Assessment Across Payment Rails To understand the blast radius of quantum cryptanalysis on payments, we must differentiate between data-in-transit, message-level non-repudiation, and long-term cryptographic archives: Rail / Protocol Classical Primitive Vulnerability Mode Quantum Blast Radius Remediation Standard SWIFT FIN / InterACT RSA-2048 / PKI Certificates Shor's Algorithm (Factorisation) Total key recovery; transaction spoofing FIPS 204 (ML-DSA-65) Dual-Signatures ISO 20022 XML Payloads XML-DSig (ECDSA P-256) Shor's Algorithm (Discrete Log) Retroactive signature forgery; payload alteration Hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 Enveloping Domestic RTGS Schemes Hardware Security Modules (PKCS#11) Firmware classical lock-in HSM root-of-trust breach; clearing disruption FIPS 140-3 Level 4 HSM Firmware with PQC Interbank TLS 1.3 Tunnels ECDHE (X25519 / secp256r1) Passive harvest-now-decrypt-later Historical packet decryption; credential leak RFC 10024 Hybrid KEM (X25519 + ML-KEM) 3. The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) Threat to Settlement Logs The most urgent misconception in financial risk management is that quantum computers present zero immediate threat because hardware is still scaling. This fails to account for adversary operational doctrine: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) represents a present-day intelligence operation whereby adversary state actors systematically record and archive encrypted wholesale payment

entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Architecture Blueprint · Sovereign CaaS Sovereign CaaS: Eliminating Custodial Counterparty Risk in Financial Institutions An architecture pattern for running a self-hosted cryptography service inside private VPCs, with an honest account of what Crypto Service Suite provides today. Sebastien Rousseau · Crypto Service Core Architecture Group Document ID: CSS-ARCH-2026-004 Classification: Technical Architecture Blueprint Standards: NIST FIPS 203/204 algorithms (not a validated module) Reference Implementation: @sebastienrousseau/crypto-server v0.0.18 Executive Abstract Engineering teams that rely only on multi-tenant cloud Key Management Services accept a dependency on a third party for key custody and availability. Teams that build their own cryptographic services take on the burden of getting the primitives, interfaces and operations right. This paper describes a middle path: a self-hosted Cryptography-as-a-Service (CaaS) tier built on @sebastienrousseau/crypto-server, deployed inside an institution's own VPC or data centre. It states what the suite provides today and what it does not. An earlier version of this paper claimed more than 100,000 operations per second, sub-millisecond signatures over HTTP/2 and gRPC, a WebAssembly SIMD engine, HSM abstraction and DORA compliance; none of those claims was supported by the code, and they have been withdrawn. Table of Contents 1. Why Self-Host Cryptographic Services 2. Service Topology & Isolation Boundaries 3. Performance 4. Key Management Backends 5. Envelope Encryption (DEK/KEK) 6. Relationship to EU DORA 7. Production Deployment 1. Why Self-Host Cryptographic Services When applications delegate key storage and signing to a third-party cloud provider, they take on risks that some institutions prefer to control directly: Jurisdiction: providers subject to foreign law (such as the US CLOUD Act) may be compelled to provide access to customer data. Vendor lock-in: each provider's KMS API differs, which complicates multi-cloud redundancy. Quotas and latency: cloud KMS endpoints apply request quotas and add a network round trip to every operation. A self-hosted service keeps key material on infrastructure the institution controls while exposing a standard interface to microservices. 2. Service Topology & Isolation Boundaries @sebastienrousseau/crypto-server is a Fastify REST service that exposes crypto-lib operations. What it provides today: 1. Ingress REST endpoints with JSON schema validation, rate limiting, security headers, and API-key or HS256 JWT authentication. There is no gRPC, HTTP/2 or built-in mTLS; terminate TLS at a proxy or load balancer. 2. Cryptographic Execution crypto-lib in the same Node.js process: FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms via @noble/post-quantum (not a validated module, no constant-time guarantee) and AES-GCM or XChaCha20-Poly1305 via @noble/ciphers. There is no WebAssembly engine. 3. Key Management No HSM integration. crypto-kms offers AWS KMS and local in-memory providers; its GCP, Azure and Vault providers are stubs and its PKCS#11 provider is a software simulation for tests. 4. Telemetry & Inventory Optional OpenTelemetry export, a Prometheus-format /metrics endpoint, structured JSON logs, and a /v2/compliance/cbom endpoint returning a CycloneDX 1.6 CBOM of the algorithms the service implements. 3. Performance No throughput or latency figures are published for crypto-server yet. The table in earlier versions of this paper (104,200 ops/sec, 0.72 ms P99 signing, comparisons with cloud KMS and hardware HSMs) was not produced by committed benchmark code and has been withdrawn. To measure primitive latency on your own hardware, run node benchmarks/crypto-bench.ts from the repository after pnpm -r run build. Load-test the REST service in your target environment before sizing a deployment. 4. Key Management Backends @sebastienrousseau/crypto-kms defines one KmsProvider interface. There is no multi-cloud broker or automatic failover. import { AwsKmsProvider } from "@sebastienrousseau/crypto-kms"; const kms = new AwsKmsProvider({ region: "eu-west-1" }); const key = await kms.createKey("aes-256-gcm", "encrypt"); const { plaintext, ciphertext } = await kms.generateDataKey(key.keyId); AWS KMS and the local in-memory provider are implemented. The GCP, Azure and HashiCorp Vault providers reject every call with Not implemented. 5. Envelope Encryption (DEK/KEK) Envelope encryption avoids encrypting large volumes of data directly under a long-lived key: Data key generation: generateDataKey() returns a fresh 256-bit data encryption key (DEK) in plaintext and wrapped under the provider's key encryption key (KEK). Data encryption: the application encrypts the record locally, for example with AES-256-GCM (96-bit nonce, 128-bit tag). Storage: the application stores the wrapped DEK next to the ciphertext and unwraps it through the KMS when needed. Memory: JavaScript cannot guarantee that

entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Strategic Research Treatise · Global Horizons The 2027 Post-Quantum Strategic Horizon & Cryptographic Audit An exhaustive technical analysis of quantum cryptanalysis timelines, lattice-based algorithms, DORA ICT risk requirements, and sovereign cryptographic resilience. Published September 28, 2026 · Sebastien Rousseau · Cryptographic Research Directorate Document ID: CSS-RES-2026-001 Classification: Executive Research Treatise Length: 28 Pages Equivalent Jurisdiction: Global Financial Markets · US CNSA 2.0 · EU DORA · UK NCSC Executive Abstract The global financial technology stack is confronting its most urgent cryptographic migration since the retirement of DES in the 1990s. With the official ratification of NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), post-quantum cryptography has transitioned from theoretical academic discourse into mandatory regulatory reality. This treatise provides an authoritative synthesis of the 2027 strategic horizon. It details why waiting until 2029 introduces existential compliance risks for financial market infrastructures, evaluates the mathematical foundations of Module-LWE and Module-SIS lattices, and presents an institutional cryptographic audit methodology designed to withstand regulatory scrutiny from central banks, the European Banking Authority, and sovereign intelligence oversight bodies. Table of Contents 1. Macroeconomic & Regulatory Timelines (2025–2030) 2. Mathematical Rigour: Lattice Hardness Reductions (M-LWE & M-SIS) 3. Physical & Micro-Architectural Side-Channel Attack Vectors 4. The Four-Tier Institutional Cryptographic Audit Framework 5. Quantitative Risk Modeling: Moscar's Theorem for Banking Records 6. Seven Critical Migration Pitfalls Observed in Tier-1 Implementations 7. Strategic Conclusions & Action Plan for Board Risk Committees 1. Macroeconomic & Regulatory Timelines (2025–2030) Regulatory authorities worldwide have converged on mandatory post-quantum migration schedules. Financial institutions operating across international borders must navigate interconnected statutory frameworks: Regulatory Body Framework / Directive Target Milestone Mandatory Requirement US NSA / White House CNSA 2.0 (NSM-10) 2026–2027 Mandatory PQC for new acquisitions; hybrid TLS 1.3 key exchange European Union DORA (Regulation EU 2022/2554) January 2025+ Continuous cryptographic risk evaluation and resilient key lifecycle governance French ANSSI PQC Advisory Recommendation 2026–2030 Mandatory hybrid encapsulation; rejection of standalone classical key exchange German BSI TR-02102-1 Cryptographic Guidelines 2026 FrodoKEM / ML-KEM recommended for long-term confidential data Bank of England / FCA Operational Resilience Policy (PS21/3) March 2025+ Mapping critical business services to vulnerable cryptographic dependencies Organizations that delay migration until 2029 risk encountering supply-chain bottlenecks for post-quantum validated Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) and severe technical debt across interconnected interbank counterparties. 2. Mathematical Rigour: Lattice Hardness Reductions NIST's standardized primary algorithms—ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204)—rely on the mathematical hardness of high-dimensional geometric lattices. Unlike RSA, which factors $N = p \cdot q$, or ECC, which solves $Q = k \cdot P$, lattice-based schemes operate in polynomial rings: $$R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[X]/(X^n + 1), \quad \text{where } n = 256 \text{ and } q = 3329$$ The core security properties derive from two problems: Module Learning With Errors (M-LWE): Finding a secret polynomial vector $\mathbf{s} \in R_q^k$ given $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}) \in R_q^{k \times k} \times R_q^k$, where $\mathbf{e}$ is a small error polynomial sampled from a centered binomial distribution. This problem reduces to the worst-case Shortest Independent Vectors Problem (SIVP) over module lattices. Module Short Integer Solution (M-SIS): Finding a non-zero vector $\mathbf{z} \in R_q^{k + \ell}$ of bounded norm $\|\mathbf{z}\| \le \beta$ such that $[\mathbf{A} \mid \mathbf{I}] \cdot \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{0} \pmod q$. The security of ML-DSA signatures guarantees existential unforgeability under chosen-message attacks (EUF-CMA). Crucially, Shor's quantum period-finding algorithm yields no speedup against lattice problems because lattice vectors do not form abelian subgroup hidden shift structures. 3. Physical & Micro-Architectural Side-Channel Attack Vectors While lattice mathematics are theoretically secure against quantum supercomputers, software implementations can be catastrophically vulnerable to physical side-channel analysis: Timing Side-Channels in Polynomial Multiplication: Standard integer divisions and non-constant-time conditional branches leak secret key coefficients. entries.content: Skip to main content Crypto Service Contact us EN ▾ Institutional Access ☰ Benchmark Specification Post-Quantum Benchmarks: Method, Sizes and Status Earlier versions of this paper published latency figures, including a WebAssembly ML-KEM-768 result of 34.1 µs, that did not come from committed code. They have been withdrawn. This page explains how to measure on your own hardware. Sebastien Rousseau · Performance Engineering Document ID: CSS-PERF-2026-006 Classification: Benchmark Method (no published results) Runtime Target: Node.js Status This paper previously reported latency and throughput figures (ML-KEM-768 encapsulation in 34.1 µs, ML-DSA-65 verification in 68.4 µs, more than 100,000 operations per second, zero garbage-collection pauses) attributed to a WebAssembly SIMD core. Those figures were not produced by any committed benchmark code, and @sebastienrousseau/crypto-wasm contains no WebAssembly. They have been withdrawn. All post-quantum operations in Crypto Service Suite run in JavaScript through @noble/post-quantum, which is not independently audited, does not guarantee constant-time execution, and is not a validated cryptographic module. No latency figures are published until they are generated by the committed benchmark code with the environment recorded. Table of Contents 1. Key, Ciphertext and Signature Sizes 2. Running the Benchmarks 1. Key, Ciphertext and Signature Sizes Sizes are fixed by the specifications, so they can be stated without measurement. They are the main practical cost of moving to lattice-based algorithms. Algorithm Mathematical Foundation Public Key Size Ciphertext / Signature Size ML-KEM-768 Module-LWE Lattice (FIPS 203) 1,184 B 1,088 B ciphertext ML-KEM-1024 Module-LWE Lattice (FIPS 203) 1,568 B 1,568 B ciphertext X25519 Curve25519 (RFC 7748) 32 B 32 B public value X25519 + ML-KEM-768 hybrid Classical + Module-LWE 1,216 B 1,120 B ciphertext RSA-3072 Integer Factorization 384 B modulus 384 B ciphertext or signature ML-DSA-65 Module Lattice (FIPS 204) 1,952 B 3,309 B signature ML-DSA-87 Module Lattice (FIPS 204) 2,592 B 4,627 B signature Ed25519 Edwards Curve (RFC 8032) 32 B 64 B signature 2. Running the Benchmarks The repository contains two benchmark entry points. The script benchmarks/crypto-bench.ts times crypto-lib operations, including ML-KEM-768 key generation and encapsulation and ML-DSA-65 key generation. The @sebastienrousseau/crypto-benchmarks harness times ML-KEM-768 encapsulation and ML-DSA-65 verification through crypto-lib against a P-256 ECDH baseline. git clone https://github.com/sebastienrousseau/crypto-service.git cd crypto-service pnpm install pnpm -r run build node benchmarks/crypto-bench.ts --iterations 500 Record the Node.js version, operating system, CPU and iteration count with any result, run on an otherwise idle machine, and repeat several times. Results depend on hardware and load and are not service level guarantees. Preferred Citation: Rousseau, S. (2026). Post-Quantum Benchmarks: Method, Sizes and Status.
